children: By N Saeed
A planned pipeline network linking Iraq with nearby Turkey and Syria will pump more than two million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil away from the perilous Hormuz Straits.
A consortium of Qatari and US companies will execute the project, which will allow Iraq to export nearly 65 percent of its pre-war oil market supplies outside Hormuz.

Qatar’s UCC is leading the consortium which also groups the oil giant Chevron and TI Capital of the US, Iraq’s oil ministry said after a meeting held at the oil ministry to discuss speeding up procedures to start the project.

The ministry said the pipelines from the southern oil-hub of Basra to Fishkhabour in Turkey and the Western Syrian port of Baniyas will have a capacity of 2.25 million bpd. Before the war between Iran and the US erupted in late February, Iraq exported nearly 3.4 million bpd through Hormuz.
Practical steps

“The meeting focused on the practical steps for the strategic export pipeline project, a major and vital project aimed at diversifying Iraq's oil export routes, with a massive export capacity estimated at 2.25 million bpd,” the ministry said.

At the end of the meeting, oil Minister Basim Khudair “directed that procedures be expedited and technical and commercial discussions intensified in order to reach the contract signing stage as soon as possible,” the ministry added.

Iraq, OPEC’s second-largest oil producer, exports more than 200,000 bpd via the northern Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline and it has plans to sharply increase that amount by transporting crude from its southern oil fields aboard tanker trucks.

Iraq is also considering building an oil pipeline to the southern Jordanian port of Aqaba. In June, an Iraqi MP delegation visited Amman for talks on the project, which has been on the cards for many years.

“Despite these projects, Iraq will remain reliant on Hormuz albeit not totally…Iraq cannot dispense with Hormuz given its proximity to China, India and other Asian markets, which account for nearly two thirds of Iraq’s oil exports,” said Waled Khaddouri, a well-known Iraq energy analyst.
Great flexibility
In comments this week, an Iraqi oil official told the state news agency that the planned pipelines would give Iraq great flexibility in exporting its crude.

“This means we will not be in the grip of Hormuz any more…once completed, they will allow Iraq to diversify export routes along with Hormuz and gradually end oil transport overland by tanker trucks,” Faisal Hamadi, director of the North Oil Company said, adding that the pipeline projects would be completed within 24-48 months.

In a recent study, the Washington Institute for Near Eastern Policy said Hormuz represents a vital crude export route for Iraq despite the high capacity of the planned pipelines through Turkey, Syria, and possible Jordan.
Asian markets
“Despite the pipeline projects, Hormuz Straits will remain key for Iraq’s crude oil exports,” the Institute said.
“Iraqi sales to Asian markets rely heavily on the strait, and efforts to establish viable alternative routes would have to overcome considerable logistical challenges.”
Amid the protracted crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, Iraq has been racing to find new outlets and methods to export its crude and petroleum products, it noted.

It said that Iraq’s economy is heavily dependent on oil revenues, which make up about 90 percent of its budget and that the majority of Iraq’s crude exports, which exceeded 3 million bpd prior to the Iran war, relied on the Strait of Hormuz, in addition to oil products such as high sulphur straight run fuel oil.

“The country’s three top oil customers over the past two years have been in Asia: China, India, and South Korea…while Iraq has major oil fields in both the northern and southern regions, it is the latter that account for the bulk of its crude exports,” it said.

“These are shipped from offshore Gulf terminals in Iraqi waters, which allow very large crude carriers (VLCCs) to load there. For these exports, the Strait of Hormuz remains critical due to the absence of an effective pipeline system that would allow substantial volumes of Basra crude produced in the southern region to be transported north and from there exported via an existing pipeline to Turkey’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan. Iraq has on several occasions spoken of plans to build new pipelines.”
(Reporting by N Saeed; Editing by Anoop Menon)
